newsitem.title: CUBA: Havana hotel's manager confirms minor explosion.
newsitem.headline: Havana hotel's manager confirms minor explosion.

text.p: A small explosion, apparently caused by a firecracker or small bomb, went off in the lobby of a central Havana hotel early on Monday.
The Spanish hotel chain that manages the Melia Cohiba in central Havana said a small explosion at 7:05 a.m. EDT (1105 GMT) had resulted in "slight material damage and no injuries."
The statement from the chain, based in Palma de Mallorca, gave no indication of what caused the explosion but said Cuban authorities were investigating.

The explosion at the Cohiba, Havana's top hotel, came just three weeks after bombs rocked the lobbies of two other hotels, the Nacional and the Capri, in the Cuban capital. They caused damage and slightly injured three people.

Dutch tourist Roberto Koppens, a guest at the Melia Cohiba, told reporters he did not see or hear the explosion but arrived in the lobby several minutes later and saw some damage to furnishings such as potted plants. Koppens said he also saw smoke and smelled powder in the lobby of the hotel.

The Melia Cohiba is owned by the Cuban state firm Cubanacan. Its director, Juan Jose de la Vega, visited the hotel during the morning but declined to confirm directly that a bomb or firecracker had gone off. Pressed to comment by reporters outside the hotel, he said, "It was a lot of noise."
Several hours after the explosion, part of the lobby of the high-rise hotel was sealed off with a wooden partition, and workmen could be heard hammering behind it.
Several uniformed and plainclothes security officials prevented people who were not guests from entering the hotel. A guard dog on a leash sat just behind the wooden partition.

The explosion on Monday coincided with an international leftist youth festival that has drawn more than 10,000 delegates from around the world to the Cuban capital. The nine-day series of discussion groups and concerts ends on Tuesday.
Most festival delegates are staying with private Cuban families or at cheaper hotels in the city.

After the small bombs that exploded at the Nacional and Capri hotels on July 12, the Cuban Interior Ministry said it had evidence that the people involved and the materials used in the bombs came from the United States.
Cuban officials have offered no more details, although it appears authorities suspect hardline Cuban exile opponents of President Fidel Castro's communist government living in the United States.
The U.S. State Department has said Havana should provide the evidence it has or stop making the accusation.
The Melia Cohiba, situated on Havana's Malecon seafront drive in the Vedado district, was allegedly the target of a small bomb in mid-April.

U.S. media reported that a bomb went off in the hotel's discotheque, but this was never confirmed by Cuban authorities. Officials of the Sol Melia chain said there had been an explosion caused by faulty gas piping.

Cuba is extremely anxious to preserve its image as a safe and orderly place to visit as it seeks to encourage the growth of tourism, a leading source of foreign exchange. Violent crime involving firearms or explosives is very rare in Cuba.
